(Sūrat al-Nāzi‘āt, also called al-Sāhirah and al-Ṭāmmah)

Its purpose is to explain the final state of man, by way of an oath concerning the resurrection of mankind and the occurrence of the Standing (al-qiyām) on the day of crowding and slipping of feet, after the complete explanation in the preceding great surahs. This alerts to the fact that the matter has reached a manifestation beyond which there is no further station. It depicts this by the extraction of souls at the hands of the noble angels; then the matter of Pharaoh the accursed and Moses, peace be upon him. Its name, al-Nāzi‘āt, is clearly suited to this aim, when the oath and its well-known answer, as understood by the leading imams, are considered. Likewise al-Sāhirah and al-Ṭāmmah, when the context is reflected upon and the arrangement for establishing harmony is attained. (In the name of Allah) the Manifest, the Hidden, the King, the All-Knowing, (the Most Merciful) who encompassed all with bounty, (the Most Compassionate) who singled out the people of His friendship with perfection, so they were specially honoured in the Abode of Peace.

* *

When He, glory be to Him, mentioned the Day on which the spirit stands and the disbeliever wishes for non-existence, He swore at the beginning of this surah by the extraction of souls in the manner He mentioned, by the hands of the angels, peace be upon them, (p-218) on account of what results from it of resurrection, and He placed it in the form of emphasis by oath, because they deny it. So He, exalted is He, said: ﴿By those who drag out﴾, that is, from among the angels — as ‘Alī and Ibn ‘Abbās, may Allah be pleased with them, said — [they drag out] the spirits and their souls from their places in the heavens, in compliance with the divine commands; ﴿with violence﴾, that is, with a forceful drawing out, with strong power, penetrating to the furthest extent of each thing in the body, even the hair, the nail and the bone, just as the archer draws the bowstring until it reaches the utmost pull. This happens to the souls of the disbelievers and the disobedient, as a barbed skewer, which is an iron rod with branching, opposing prongs, is drawn out of wet wool. Ibn Jarīr, as is his habit, generalised in regard to everything the word can bear, and said: "The correct view is that it should be said: Allah, exalted is He, did not specify; so every drawing-out is included in His oath," meaning, taking heed of what Allah has given them of power for that extraction, which indicates the perfection of wisdom and the capacity to do what He, glory be to Him, wills.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 79, verse 2:

When he mentioned the violent extraction (al-shadd), beginning with it because it is more terrifying, he followed it with gentleness, saying: ﴿And those who extract gently﴾ — meaning those that draw out, gently, the souls, or their wings, from their places ﴿with gentleness﴾ — meaning gently, so that it does not leave off, even though the attachment between the spirit and the body is gentle, just as a thing is untied (yanshitu) from a tether (iqal), meaning it is loosened from a knot that had been tied in the form of a slipknot (unshuta). Al-Farra' said: "I heard the Arabs say: 'nashatu al-iqal' when I untied it, and 'anshatu' when I tied it with a slipknot," — end of quote. Also, al-nashat means pulling and drawing out; it is said: "I drew the bucket out (nashatu al-dalw nashtan)" when you drew it out. Al-Khalil said: al-nashat and al-infashat is your pulling a thing toward yourself until it comes loose. This applies to the souls of the people of obedience. Likewise, nazaʿa (to pull out) is used for plants, and inshaʾ and inmaʾ for everything whose pulling out is intended, or he made it active (nashsha·ahu). So the One who empowered some of His servants to do this, which involves distinguishing souls from others, given their subtlety and intense mixing, is able to distinguish the body of every living being from the body of another, after each has become dust and mixed with the dust of the other.

The Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 79, verse 3:

When he (al-Biqa'i) had mentioned the two types of the (al-sull, the) extractors/drawers (of souls) with severity and gentleness, he mentioned their action in their approach to it (the soul) and their withdrawal from it, so he said: ﴿And those who glide swiftly﴾ [i.e. - ] from the angels also, in the air, after they have prepared themselves for flight, to whatever orders God has commanded them from His commands, from the Spirit or others, ﴿gliding swiftly﴾ — it is at the utmost speed, because there is no impediment to them; rather [indeed - ] God has enabled them to pass through everything, just as He has enabled the swimmer in water and air. For this reason He joined to it with (the particle) fa' (then/so) His saying:

Al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on Surah 79, verse 4:

﴿Fa-as-sabiqati﴾ meaning: after their swimming through flight toward what they were commanded to do, namely plunging souls into bliss or into hellfire, or other things they were commanded to do, [they proceed] more swiftly than a glance, with power and dominance over everything that they attempt, [racing] ﴿in a race﴾ (p-220)

When this became clear, the excellence of their obedience to the commands was made evident, and with it the magnitude of their consideration of consequences. This is indicated by the *fa'* (the particle of consequence) in His saying ﴿*fa-l-mudabbirāti*﴾, meaning: the ones who contemplate the backs (final outcomes) of affairs and their consequences, in order to perfect what they were commanded regarding the souls and other things, ﴿*amran*﴾, meaning: a great matter. It is also valid that these oaths refer to the sun, the moon, the stars, the winds, and the horses swimming in the earth and the air, for the benefit of the servants and the management of their affairs, some of them preceding others. Some of the exegetes said this. The answer (*jawāb*) of the oath is omitted, to indicate that the knowledge of it is so manifest, through the indication of what precedes and follows it, that it reaches a limit beyond which nothing more is needed. It is so evident that there is no need to mention it, so it was omitted, just as affirming it is done by proof. Its estimated form is: "You will surely be taken away from the world in which you are deluded; We will pull out its state and sever its joints." For all that has preceded of the works of Our angels is from the preliminaries of that, as a refutation of the saying of the disbelievers: ﴿*There is nothing but our life of this world: we die and we live, and nothing destroys us except time*﴾ [al-Jathiyah: 24], referred to by their question about it, because it was in the manner of mockery and denial: ﴿*When will the Hour come?*﴾ or ﴿*Indeed, you will be resurrected after death and the ending of this abode*﴾? Then ﴿*you will surely be recompensed for what you have done*﴾, through existing causes prepared among you, which We have arranged and brought into being when We brought this worldly life into existence, even if you do not see them. Likewise, these matters which We have told you about, in the drawing out of souls, the growth of plants, and the benefits, exist among you (p-221), and the dead person is nearest to you, while they (the angels) carry out their works. The dying person makes the loudest sound and the greatest movement, and then he subsides and becomes still after that matter, falls silent, his limbs stretch out, and he dies, and he departs from you by compulsion, and what passed has passed, as if it had never been, and it did not prevail in any time of the times, by those causes which carry out their works, extend their ropes, anchor their weights, and cast their terrors and fears, while you do not see them. Then, how wondrous it is that all this, despite its abundance, does not prevent you from deeming it unlikely, in His power, that He could distinguish the dust of one body from the dust of another body.

Abu Ja'far ibn al-Zubayr said: When Surat al-Naba' made clear the state of the disbeliever in His saying ﴿*Would that I were dust*﴾ [al-Naba': 40], upon seeing what his hands had sent forward, and witnessing the great punishment he sees, and after mentioning the detailed states and terrors, it followed that with what his state had been in his worldly life of deeming his return in the Hereafter unlikely. It mentioned that this is near for Him, glory be to Him, as He said in another place: ﴿*And it is easier for Him*﴾ [al-Rum: 27], and this is with respect to us and what we are accustomed to; otherwise, nothing is easier or harder for Him, glory be to Him: ﴿*His command, when He intends a thing, is only that He says to it, "Be," and it is*﴾ [Ya-Sin: 82]. So He said, exalted is He: ﴿*By those who drag out with violence*﴾ [al-Nazi'at: 1] up to His saying: ﴿*They say, "Shall we indeed be returned to our former state?"*﴾ [al-Nazi'at: 10] ﴿*"Even when we are decayed bones?"*﴾ [al-Nazi'at: 11], as they deem this unlikely and push it away. ﴿*It will be but one blast*﴾ [al-Nazi'at: 13], meaning one cry, ﴿*and immediately they will be on the surface of the earth*﴾ [al-Nazi'at: 14], meaning the earth, standing, looking (p-222) at what their hands have sent forward, wishing that they had been dust, and that does not benefit them. Then He, exalted is He, mentioned from the story of Pharaoh and his tyranny what suits the situation with the intent of admonition and taking lessons. For this reason He followed the story with His saying, glory be to Him: ﴿*Indeed, in that is a lesson for whoever fears*﴾ [al-Nazi'at: 26]. End.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 79, verse 6:

When He swore by the performance of those great acts, which none is capable of performing except the King, the All-Knowing, He mentioned the signs that will accompany them, to magnify the matter of the Hour, because souls are inclined to what they perceive with their senses, while unseen things are forgotten and neglected by them. So He said, taking as the object of the adverbial phrase the omitted element (because, owing to its great clarity, it is as if it were pronounced [therein]): ﴿On the Day the quaking one quakes﴾, that is, it will shake with a great and disturbing trembling. ﴿The quaking one﴾, that is, the Blast, which is the First Blast, of such a kind that it reaches—by the intensity of its shaking of hearts and of all still things, from the earth and the mountains, to the extraction of souls from all the people of the earth—a degree that makes it deserving of being described as foremost in quaking. Al-Baghawi said: The root of ar-raj fah (the quaking) is sound and movement.

When he mentioned the first Blast, he followed it with the second as a circumstance (ḥāl) of it, indicating its nearness in a figurative sense (p. 223), since the occurrence is certain, and because all of that is in the judgment (ḥukm -) of one day. So the coming of the circumstance is valid even though its time is distant from the time of the one it accompanies. Thus He said: ﴿The Following One follows it﴾, meaning the Blast that follows it, by which all the dead will stand and the scattered bones will be gathered, and by whose terror the earth and the heavens will be shaken, the mountains will be crushed, and the great quake will occur. From it will come the movement after the coming to the heaped-up sand dune, [and similar -] that of the severe and lengthy affair. Ḥamzah al-Kirmānī said: al-Suddī narrated from Abū Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him, that when people die at the first Blowing (al-nafkhah), Allah will send down upon them water from beneath the Throne, called the Water of Life, and they will sprout from it as crops sprout from water. When their bodies are complete, the spirit will be breathed into them. Then He will cast upon them a sleep, and while they are in their graves, the Trumpet will be blown a second time, and they will sit up, finding the taste of sleep in their heads and eyes.

When He mentioned the Resurrection (al-ba'th), He mentioned the state of those who deny it, because the context is about them. So He began with an indefinite noun described by a qualifier, saying: ﴿Hearts, on that Day﴾, i.e., when the creatures stand up at the second Blast that follows the first, ﴿will be trembling﴾, i.e., their inner parts (ajwaf) will be violently agitated, fearful, nearly leaping out of them from the intensity of the pounding (al-wajib, the violent throbbing of the heart).

When He had described them as trembling, and its cause might be hidden, since it can occur at great joy just as it can occur at intense dread, He informed of what confirms its meaning, saying: ﴿Their eyes﴾, that is, the eyes of their owners, so this is an instance of istikhdam (a figure of speech in which a pronoun is made to refer to one sense of a word while another sense is intended), ﴿humbled﴾, that is, abased, with the abasement visible upon them, and the agitation of hearts from the evil of their condition; and for this reason He attributed it to them.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 79, verse 10:

When He described them with agitation and humiliation, He gave the reason for it, so that from it one would know that whoever says the opposite of their saying will have the opposite of their description, namely steadiness, tranquility and apparent might. So He said: ﴿They say﴾, that is, in the worldly life, a saying they renew at every moment, without fear or shame, out of mockery and denial.

﴿Are we indeed going to be returned﴾, that is, after death, by one who has the attribute of returning us, whoever he may be, ﴿to the original state (al-hafirah)﴾, that is, to the life in which we were before death, which is our first condition. It is from their saying: "So-and-so returned along his hafirah," meaning his path which he came by and which he dug, that is, he left an impression upon it by his walking, just as feet and hooves leave marks on roads. The active participle was used for the passive (mafʿūlah) as an intensification, and that is its real meaning. Then it was said of one who was in a matter, then left it and then returned to it: "He returned to his hafirah."

(p-225) It was also said: al-hafirah is the earth, which is the place of the hooves.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 79, verse 11:

When he had described their hearts by this denial, which is such that its perpetrator ought to melt with shame if he commits it even once, and had indicated the intensity of their impudence by its repetition, he followed it with an explicit statement of their repeated making of this denial, in a manner that points to the cause (al-'illah) that drove them to their saying. That saying is their words: ﴿Even when we are bones, decayed?﴾ That is, "when we have come to a state that has become our innate nature (jibillah)." ﴿Decayed bones (ʿiẓāman nakhirah)﴾ means that they are at the utmost point of crumbling, until they disintegrate. Thus decay, which is wasting away, disintegration and shattering, became as though it were a natural disposition (ṭubi'a) imprinted upon them, and they were imprinted with it. They are the hardest part of the body, so how about what is other than them of the frame? And according to the reading "nākhirah" (with the alif), the meaning is that they have been emptied of what was in them, so that the air whistles through them, that is, makes a sound.

When the element governing "idhā" (then) is understood as something like: "Will we be returned at that time to our first state and stand up as we were?", the verb of the omitted clause is indicated by His words, exalted be He, about them: ﴿They said﴾, meaning once, on one occasion: ﴿That﴾, that is, the return to the first state, which is very strange and far from reason in their assumption, ﴿then﴾, that is, if we are returned to our first life with nothing for us, just as we were born with nothing for us, and we lose everything we strove to acquire, gather, and accumulate. ﴿a losing return﴾, that is, a return, a restoration, and a turning back. ﴿losing﴾, that is, it is so great a loss for us, by what we have lost of what we obtained of the [state and-] outcome and good qualities (p-226), that it is deeply entrenched in loss, so that it is as if it itself were the one that loses. Perhaps He expressed it in the past tense because they permitted themselves this saying only once in a lifetime, whereas the usual form of their saying was that, upon the supposition of resurrection, they would be happier than the believers by the measure of their condition in this world, and similar to this of lies against God.

Since the implied sense was: "Yes, by God, you will surely be brought back, O people. What you are saying is all a matter of your deeming it far-fetched, even though you would admit its ease if you reasoned soundly. As for the matter of power, initiation is harder than restoration, and you already admit initiation. Also, if the deeming it far-fetched arises from the supposition that one who has become dust cannot return, because his dust cannot be distinguished from the dust of others, then the angels' distinguishing of the one who draws out and the one who is drawn out, that is, the soul from the body, is far harder than that, and likewise other affairs the angels manage. How, then, could anything be hard for their Lord, glorified is He, when its like is easy for them? As for the matter of customs, no one leaves his subjects without any reckoning at all. As for the matter of the promise, it has already been given, and it is not among the characteristics of the noble, much less of kings, to break a promise or to allow injustice. So do not deny it, and do not find it difficult." He said, giving the cause of this implied sense and warning the doubters who follow blindly: ﴿Then it will be but a single shout﴾, that is, the Resurrection, ﴿a single shout﴾, that is, a cry with a rebuke that contains the command to rise, the driving to the place of assembly, and the prohibition of lagging behind. ﴿A single shout﴾ (p-227) He expressed it with *zajr* (rebuke), which is stronger than *nahy* (prohibition), because it is used for a summons, since it is a cry from which rising cannot lag behind at all. It was as if the tongue of the state said to that cry: "O decayed bodies! Cease your slumber, rise to the appointed time, by the resurrection We have decreed, for the time of harvest has ended, and the time of gathering the provision one has sent ahead has come. Woe, then, to him who has no provision!"

Then (﴿فَإذا هُمْ﴾) means: as a consequence of this blast, which is the second, they will be startled with extreme speed, being alive and standing ﴿in the Sahirah﴾, that is, upon the surface of the white, level, wide earth which Allah will renew for the recompense. Its vastness will be such that it is as if it had swallowed them, despite their great number, which exceeds counting and surpasses limit. It was named thus because water flows in it from the Sahirah, which is the flowing spring; or because whoever traverses it stays awake (yasharu) out of fear, just as sleep is a state of safety; or because in this particular land there is no sleep, given the long standing and the alternation of calamities that bring about death.

When the story of Moses, upon him be prayer and peace, with the Copts (al-Qibt) occurred, it was most similar to the Resurrection, because of the transformations and changes that took place in it, and the bringing into existence of things that did not exist, such as the locusts, the lice, and the frogs, in those forms that were outside the usual customs, in the swiftest time. It involved the subjugation of the tyrants and the bestowing of favour upon the weak, until the final outcome was that (p-228) He gathered the Children of Israel, and He made them leave the Copts in a gentle, easy departure, all of them, together with all their possessions and their animals [to their Lord], and He gathered all the Copts behind them, and He uprooted them, all of them, through Pharaoh's gathering of them, by the voices of the callers on his behalf, in the swiftest time and the easiest affair, to their destruction, just as the dead are gathered after their revival by the Blast to the al-Sahirah (the open plain of the Resurrection). Then the outcome for the two groups was, by the decree of those who arrange the affair, that the Children of Israel were saved by the sea, just as the believers will be saved on the Day of Resurrection by the al-Sirat (the bridge over Hell), and Pharaoh and his people were destroyed by it, just as the disbelievers fall from the al-Sirat. This is because he saw Pharaoh and his troops, when the sea had split for the Children of Israel, and they did not take heed from that. Then they entered it behind them, and they did not think it possible that He who had removed it from its place was able to return it as He had originated it, so that He drowned them, and they persisted in their blindness until God returned it, and He drowned them in it. Likewise, whoever denies the Resurrection sees God's beginning of him and of others, and His annihilating them after bringing them into being. Then he does not hold it possible that He should return them as He began them the first time. With this is connected His, may He be exalted, saying in answer to one who says: "Is there any proof of that?" addressing the most noble of creation, as a sign that none but you truly takes heed of this as it should be taken, asking a question (of the interrogative form) for alerting and for urging the self to gather itself for reflection, contemplation, and taking heed, affirming and consoling him, may (ﷺ), and threatening those who deny, that their condition should be—though they are the weakest people on earth, since they have no king—like the condition of Pharaoh in this matter, though he was the strongest people on earth, through the kingship he possessed, the multitude and strength of his troops, his sorcery, and his deceptive wiles in their deceit and their cunning. He saw signs that no one had seen before him. When he persisted in denial, did not return, and the discipline did not benefit him, God drowned him and his household, and He left none of them, although they could not be counted in number, to the extent that it was said that his vanguard alone was equal in number to the Children of Israel, six hundred thousand. ﴿Has there come to you the story of Moses?﴾ That is, O most knowing of creation, the account of his affair which We renewed for him when We willed him, so that it will be sufficient for you in consolation, and for your people in urging belief, alerting to taking heed, and threatening against denial and persistence.

﴿When﴾, that is, at the time when ﴿his Lord called to him﴾, that is, the One who had shown him favour [to him] by bringing him into being, bringing him near, and directing him, ordained his sending and decreed it, ﴿in the sacred valley﴾, that is, the purified valley, purified to the utmost degree, by God's honouring him with the descent of prophethood, which pours forth blessings. Then He clarified it by His saying: ﴿Tuwa﴾. It is the valley in which He folded away evil from the Children of Israel and from whomever of His creation He willed, and in which He spread the blessings of prophethood over all the people of the earth, [the one who] becomes a Muslim by his Islam, and [others] by the lifting of the punishment of annihilation (ʿadhab al-istiʾṣāl) from them. For the scholars said: the punishment of the grave (ʿadhab al-qabr), that is, the punishment of annihilation, was lifted when the Torah was sent down. (p-٢٣٠)

It is a valley at al-Tur, between Aylah (Eilat) and Misr (Egypt).

When he mentioned the call, he explained its fruit with his words, beginning a new sentence (*isti'naf*) to alert the people of desire, the self-impressed and the arrogant. The context indicates that the implied meaning is: he called to him, saying: ﴿Go to Pharaoh﴾, that is, the king of Egypt who had enslaved the Children of Israel, and who, having become fearful of one of them, began slaughtering their sons out of fear of him. That one was you. We raised you in his house for his destruction, so that he would know that there is no escape from Our decree. Thus you became the most honoured of the Children of Israel. The cause of his destruction was present with him in his house, within his sight and hearing, while he did not perceive it. Then you killed a man from among them and left their land in fear, watching out (for pursuit).

When He commanded him to go to him, He gave a reason that entails Pharaoh's destruction at his hands, peace be upon him, as a sign of good tidings to him that Pharaoh has no power over him. For this reason He emphasised the command, because a matter of this kind is one that human nature tends to hesitate about. So He said: ﴿Indeed he has transgressed﴾, that is, he exceeded the limit and went beyond bounds, so he deserved to be met with seriousness. Then, as a consequence of going to him, He said:

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 79, verse 18:

﴿So say﴾, that is, to him, as an elaboration on some of what preceded in Surah Ta-Ha regarding gentleness of speech and tenderness in the invitation in address: ﴿Would you like﴾, that is, do you have an inclination and need ﴿to purify yourself﴾, that is, to adorn yourself with virtues and cleanse yourself of vices, even with the least kind of purification: outward and inward purity, which brings about growth and abundance, and the conveying of the lesser by what the dropping of the taʼ of the tafaʻʻul form indicates, which implies lightening (takhfif). This is by submission (idhʻan), which entails faith, and the sending of the Children of Israel. The two Hijazi readers (Ibn Kathir and Abu ʻAmr) and Yaʻqub read it with shaddah (tashdid), that is, a thorough purification, because whoever enters into purification at the hand of a perfect person, especially a prophet of the ulu al-ʻazm (the resolute messengers), is close to reaching the utmost limit in purity.

When he indicated to him purification from shirk, he followed it with the deeds, saying: ﴿And I will guide you﴾, i.e., I will make clear to you, after purification through faith, which is the foundation: the way of travel ﴿to your Lord﴾, i.e., the One who brought you into existence, who was good to you, and who nurtured you by making known to you the deeds that please Him and the traits that anger Him, after He had granted you in this world the utmost of your hopes. ﴿So that you fear﴾, i.e., as a consequence of that, you will come to act as one who fears His punishment with great fear, so you fulfill the obligations, abandon the prohibited acts and all other forbidden things, and thus you attain the highest ranks of purification, combining the kingdom of the Hereafter with the kingdom of this world. For fear is what drives one to every good, while feeling secure is what drives one to evil.

The implied sense is: he went to him as God had commanded, and said [to him -] that, and [Pharaoh] asked for proof of the validity of the message, finding it hard to believe that he would be singled out from among them for this lofty rank, even though [Moses] had raised him as a child. ﴿So he showed him﴾, that is, as a consequence of his request, [Moses] proved his truthfulness by showing him ﴿the sign﴾, that is, the indication of that, ﴿the greatest﴾. This was the turning of the staff into a serpent, or all of his miracles (mu'jizat).

The commentary is on Q. 79:21, "But he denied and disobeyed."

﴿فَكَذَّبَ﴾ — i.e., it resulted from seeing that (the sign), that he committed denial (al-takdhib) regarding something which, upon being seen, ought to call for affirmation (al-tasdiq). ﴿وعَصى﴾ — i.e., he committed disobedience (al-'isyan), which is great refusal (al-iba') and arrogance (al-takabbur) against complying with what he was called to, combined with denial, after the proof of truthfulness had been established and the matter had been verified.

Since persistence in denial is more severe when it comes from someone who has seen and recognized the truth, especially when he is great and this is quite unlikely, He indicated it with the particle of delay (thumma), which also indicates the reality of delay, and said: ﴿Then he turned his back﴾, meaning Pharaoh, after the respite and forbearance, turned away with a great turning-away, persisting in an even greater rebellion than what he had been in, after momentous calamities and lengthy witnessings. ﴿Striving﴾, meaning he exerted his utmost effort, acting like one who hastens with the utmost haste to nullify the divine command, through his scanty intellect and corrupt opinion, and refused to accept the truth.

Surah 79, verse 23 (al-Biqa'i, Nazm al-Durar):

﴿Then he gathered [his people]﴾, i.e., as a consequence of his turning away, he strove, and there followed from that that he gathered the magicians willingly and unwillingly, and he also added to them his soldiers. ﴿Then he called out﴾, i.e., in the assemblies.

﴿So he said﴾: that is, his herald, who had no doubt that it came from him, so his saying was like his saying: ﴿I am your Lord, the Most High﴾. Ḥamzah al-Karmānī said: Mūsā (عليه السلام) said to him: "Indeed my Lord has sent me to you. If you believe in your Lord, you will remain four hundred years in joy and bliss, and then you will die and enter Paradise." He said: "Let me consult Hāmān." So he consulted him, and Hāmān said: "Will you become a servant after you were a lord who was worshipped?" At that, he sent for the police and gathered the magicians and the soldiers. When they had assembled, the enemy of Allah stood upon his throne and said: "I am ﴿your Lord, the Most High﴾." So this was his proclamation, meaning: all of you are lords, some of you above others, and I am the highest of you, and there is no lord above me at all. This is because the god, in his view, is nature (al-ṭabīʿah), which is divided among existing things, so they are all lords, and whoever is higher has more right to command, and he was higher than them. So Allah cursed him, condemned him, and cursed whoever follows his school of thought, such as Ibn ʿArabī, Ibn al-Fāriḍ and their followers, since they denied the Chooser, the King, the Subduer, and His Messenger, the chosen and selected one, and in the doctrine of the unity of existence (waḥdat al-wujūd) they followed some of the philosophers, then al-Ḥallāj after Pharaoh. This one (Pharaoh) is one about whom Allah did not explicitly condemn anyone as He explicitly condemned him, nor did He explicitly state the wretchedness of anyone as He explicitly stated his wretchedness, as in this verse, for it explicitly states the befalling of his punishment in the Hereafter just as it befell him in this world. [And] His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So We seized him and his soldiers and cast them into the sea. Look, then, at the end of the wrongdoers﴾ [al-Qaṣaṣ: 40]. ﴿And We made them leaders calling to the Fire, and on the Day of Resurrection they will not be helped﴾ [al-Qaṣaṣ: 41]. ﴿And We followed them in this world with a curse, and on the Day of Resurrection they will be among the disfigured﴾ [al-Qaṣaṣ: 42].

And besides these there are many other clear signs and manifest proofs that cannot be counted, and the greatest of them is the self-evident analogy (al-qiyās al-badīhī) in its conclusion: ﴿Indeed Pharaoh was haughty in the land, and indeed he was among the transgressors﴾ [Yūnus: 83], and ﴿Indeed the transgressors are the companions of the Fire﴾ [Ghāfir: 43]. It is related that when Iblīs heard this statement of his, he said: "I acted arrogantly toward Ādam, and I suffered what I suffered, and this one says this?" It was pride that drove him to this, arising from the trial of ease, in which patience is greater than patience in hardship. Al-Imām al-Ghazālī said in the Book of Patience from the Iḥyāʾ: "Patience in obedience is difficult, because the soul by its nature shrinks from servitude and craves lordship. For this reason some of the knowers said: There is no soul but that it conceals what Pharaoh manifested in his saying ﴿I am your Lord, the Most High﴾, but Pharaoh found room and acceptance for it, so he manifested it when he made his people feel contemptible, and they obeyed him. And there is no one but that he claims this with his servant, his attendant, his followers and everyone under his domination and obedience, even if he refrains from displaying it, for his displeasure and rage when they fall short in serving him arise only from concealed pride and a contest for lordship under the cloak of greatness." End of quotation. (p-٢٣٥) This is confirmed by the fact that the Prophet ﷺ never rebuked his servant for anything at all. And Allah, exalted is He, is the One who grants success to what is right.

When God, glory be to Him, reported of him this shameful word that disparages the king, and kings cannot tolerate such a thing in any way, He made the punishment follow from it and linked His words: ﴿So God seized him﴾, that is, the king who has no equal and to whom no one shares authority, seized him with a seizing of subjugation and humiliation, making him an example and disgracing him, ﴿the punishment of the Hereafter﴾. It is a verbal noun (maṣdar) from the sense of the sentence, meaning a seizing of exemplary punishment in it, which becomes a lesson by which whoever hears of a case like Pharaoh's is restrained and admonished. He placed "the Hereafter" first to give attention to its matter and to indicate that the greatness of its punishment is greater, and that a person tastes it only when the veil of this world is lifted by death. It also serves as a warning that preventing such a claim is more possible when it is made by one who is truthful about it. This ordering is not for the sake of the rhyme (fāṣila), because if it had been said "the other [punishment]" (al-ukhrā), it would have agreed with ﴿and the first﴾, meaning the punishment of this world, which comes before the Hereafter. Whoever hears the story of his drowning and of all that befell him, that would be for him an exemplary punishment preventing anyone from doing the like of it or something less than it.

Al-Ḍaḥḥāk said: As for in this world, God, exalted is He, drowned him and cast him onto a high place of the earth. As for in the next world, God, exalted is He, will cause him to enter the Fire and will make him appear upon a mound of it, shackled and bound, and it will be proclaimed over him: "This is the one who claimed lordship (rubūbiyya) apart from God." End of quotation.

I have no doubt that al-Ḥallāj, Ibn ʿArabī and Ibn al-Fāriḍ, and their followers, will be in the Fire beneath them and beneath their family, drinking their essence. For they claimed that he was saved and affirmed him in what he claimed, and they claimed for themselves and for others the like of what he claimed, as a denial of the Qur'an and an extreme of transgression. They went further than him by making common the Greatest Name (al-ism al-aʿẓam), which God protected from being claimed by anyone before the sending of the Prophet (ﷺ). They claimed that it applies to them and to every person, indeed to everything. The sign of this wicked sect, which never fails, is that if you say to one of them: "Curse Pharaoh, on whom all the communities have agreed to curse," he hesitates. Pharaoh is for them a model of evil and wickedness, so he does not curse him, and if he does curse him, it is only after a pause.

When Glorified and Exalted God summarized the stories of the past in these few words, He did so in the best and most concise manner, without contradicting anything of what had gone before. This is because the detailed portion (al-mufaṣṣal, the later short surahs of the Qur'an) is the proper place for brevity. As for its order of revelation, it was revealed first, so bringing the stories closer to people by limiting them to what is necessary was better, so that they would find them familiar. As for its order in the arrangement, it is to remind them of what came before, so that it gathers [in -] the imagination in the shortest time, and so that the extended account is recalled through it. He concluded it with this strange way of taking [the stories], guiding [to] what the story contains of lessons, while pointing to the recollection of all that came before. He said, emphasizing and confirming it for the one who denies and alerting the one who believes:

﴿Indeed, in that﴾, that is, in the great matter that He did and in what was done to them, ﴿is a lesson﴾, that is, a great matter [-] which one deliberately takes as a lesson, moving from one meaning to another, until one arrives thereby at many of the forms of knowledge, ﴿for whoever fears﴾, that is, whoever by nature has great fear of God. This is because fear, as was mentioned previously, is the foundation of all good. The first step of crossing over is that the listener transfers the condition of others to himself, and so he recalls the rescue of the Children of Israel despite their weakness relative to their enemies, then the power that their oppressors had over them, to the point that it made [Pharaoh] pursue them with his armies, then the splitting of the sea, then [Pharaoh's] bringing them [into the sea], then their drowning in it in the blink of an eye. None of them went out to report the power of God to bring the disbelievers into the Fire and to subdue every tyrant, nor [to report] turning the staff into a serpent, nor bringing out lice and frogs from the earth, nor turning water into blood. (p-٢٣٨) [His] power, Glorified and Exalted is He, over that, [and over] punishing the listener and other than him, and over the especially [matter] of resurrection, and beyond that of the lessons [-] is of clear effect.

Al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 79, verse 27:

When he had concluded the story of Pharaoh, may Allah curse him, with the lesson, and the greatest lesson in it was the complete power (of Allah), especially over the resurrection, as is indicated by its beginning and its end, and (the lesson of) the punishment for denying it, because denying it gathers all of evil, while affirming it gathers all of good, and they were deeming it far-fetched because of their deeming power over it far-fetched, he connected to it what is like its result. So He said, establishing (the point), addressing those who harbour doubt and are skeptical, placing them in a position of (having to affirm) power, rebuking them for their deeming it far-fetched. This is a turn, after restricting the address to him (ﷺ) because of the subtlety of his understanding and the nobility of his knowledge (ﷺ), to the general address, because the clarity of this proof is evident to every human being, appealing to them in reproach: ﴿Are you more difficult to create﴾, that is, O living ones, despite being a weak creation, ﴿or the heaven?﴾ That is, more difficult and heavier in terms of measuring and bringing into existence, ﴿or the heaven﴾, with all its vastness, greatness, height and benefits.

And since the answer was definitely "the heaven," (the speaker) pointed to the greatest of what is seen, because the human world is an abridgement of the outer world, and the outer world has the added quality of long endurance together with not being affected. He connected to it His saying, as evidence of His power over resurrection, since His power over what is greater than it (implies power over what is lesser), because the One Who was able to originate the greater is even more able to re-create the lesser, explaining the manner of His creating it: ﴿He raised it﴾, that is, He made it a canopy over the earth with all its greatness. Then he explained the construction with His saying:

ﷺ

﴿He raised its height﴾ [i.e.] He made the measure of its elevation above the earth, or its thickness extending upward, elevated. In the Qamus (the dictionary of al-Firuzabadi) it says: al-samk means the ceiling, or the distance from the top of a house to its bottom, or the height of anything. Abu Hayyan said: al-samk is the elevation between the surface of the sky that is nearest to us and its surface that lies beyond it. ﴿And He made it level﴾, i.e., He balanced it afterwards, by making it even, with nothing in it higher or lower than anything else, and without any fissure in it. He set it in order by that with which its perfection was completed, namely the stars and other things. And He made the thickness of each sky, and the distance between every two skies, and the thickness of each earth, and the distance between every two earths, equal, so that none of these exceeds another at all.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 79, verse 29:

When each of these things indicates the power to resurrect, because it is the bringing into existence of something greater than the creation of a human being from nothing, he followed it with what conceives of resurrection in every day and night twice, saying: ﴿And He darkens its night﴾, meaning He makes it dark with a darkness through which one cannot find the way to what was there in the state of light, ﴿its night﴾, meaning by the disappearance of its sun, so He conceals its light by the extension of the earth's shadow over everything the sun had appeared upon. He attributed it to the day (ليل, "its night") because it is renewed by its movement, and he began with it because it came first, and non-existence precedes existence (p-240) ﴿and brings forth its forenoon﴾, by the rising of its sun, so it lights its daytime. The verse is of the type of ihtibak (concealment by mutual implication): by ﴿darkens﴾ it indicates ﴿lights﴾, and by bringing forth the forenoon it indicates the concealment of the light. Perhaps he expressed the day by the forenoon (ضحى) because it is its brightest part and strongest in light.

When he began with the indication of the upper world, because it is more indicative of the wonders and benefits it contains, along with its being more noble, he mentioned that He perfected the sky, which is like the male, and then followed this by stating that He arranged what is for it like the female, saying: ﴿And the earth﴾. Since the intended meaning is the encompassing of time through the continuation of spreading out, he omitted the preposition and said: ﴿after that﴾, i.e., after all that has been mentioned, ﴿He spread it out﴾, i.e., He extended and stretched it out for habitation and the rest of its benefits, after He had created it and brought it into existence before the creation of the sky, not yet arranged in act nor spread out.

When He spread it out, He followed that with what it entails of benefits, since the intended dwelling depends on the spreading. So He said, as an explanation of it without a conjunction: ﴿He brought forth from it﴾, that is, from the earth, ﴿its water﴾ by making the springs gush forth. Attributing the water to the earth indicates that it is within it. ﴿And its pasture﴾, which comes forth by means of the water. What is meant is that which is grazed, its place and its time.

Having mentioned the earth and its benefits, he mentioned the anchors through which its benefit is completed, so He said: ﴿And the mountains﴾, that is, specifically, ﴿He set them firmly﴾, that is, He fixed them and made them stable, [and -] together with their being firm and not shifting, for indeed He, glory be to Him, made them anchors for the earth, a cause of its steadiness, just as anchors are a cause of the ship's steadiness.

When the renewal was already evident from the animal's taking of food, drink and other provisions, for whenever something is lost from it, it takes what has been decreed for it so as to restore that or part of it, He said, drawing attention to the fact that it is every day in renewal, building as a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) upon what preceded in its decreed measure: "as a provision" (matā'an), decreed, ﴿for you﴾, enjoying through what is in it of benefits, ﴿and for your cattle﴾, that is, your livestock, through grazing and other things.

When he had mentioned what points to the Resurrection, he followed it with what occurs as a consequence of the Resurrection, as a sign that existence was created only for the sake of the Resurrection, since it is the place where wisdom is fulfilled: ﴿So when the Greatest Calamity comes﴾, that is, after death, ﴿the Greatest Calamity﴾, that is, the great catastrophe which overwhelms (taṭumm, i.e., rises above and covers) all other calamities and eclipses them, so that it is the greatest calamity that exists, namely the Resurrection by the second blast of the Trumpet, as Ibn ʿAbbas (may Allah be pleased with them both) said. The element governing "idhā" (its governing verb, ʿāmil) is omitted, and its estimated meaning is: He will separate people into the wretched and the happy.

Since a thing's magnitude is not known when it is absent except through what occurs in it, He said, substituting for it: ﴿The day man will remember what he strove for﴾ [i.e., a great and manifest remembrance], by that which the manifestation (al-izhar) pointed to. ﴿Man﴾, i.e., the created being who is familiar with himself and heedless of that for which he was created. ﴿What he strove for﴾, i.e., all his deeds, both good and evil, because he sees it in the record of his deeds. The report about his remembering, while alerting to the gravity that lies in that [day], is because no one exerts his utmost effort in remembering except for something that compels him to it, namely the reckoning and its recording in the record of his deeds.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 79, verse 36:

When he had pointed to the Reckoning, he mentioned what follows it, saying: ﴿And Hellfire is brought forth﴾, meaning it is made manifest in a great manifestation. He put the verb in the passive form because the terrifying matter is the general fact of its being brought forth, not that it is brought forth by a specific agent, along with the indication of ease and facility, since this is the manner of [speech -] those who have power. ﴿Al-Jahim﴾, that is, the Fire whose blaze and heat have grown intense. ﴿For whoever sees﴾, meaning whoever he may be, because nothing stands between anyone and seeing it. However, the one who is saved does not turn his gaze toward it, so he does not see it, as Allah the Exalted said: ﴿They will not hear its faintest sound﴾ [al-Anbiya': 102].

Since the answer to "idhā" (when), as has passed, is omitted, and its implied sense is that He divided people into two groups—a group for the Hellfire and a group for the Bliss—Exalted is He said, causing this to follow and detailing it: ﴿Then as for he who transgressed﴾, meaning he who exceeded the limit in aggression and so did not fear the standing before his Lord. He said in al-Qamus: "Taghā: he went beyond the measure and rose up [and —] taghā: he exceeded in disbelief, and was extravagant in sins and wrongdoing; and the water: it rose up."

Since what comes after the limits of God is the worldly life, he stated it explicitly, saying: ﴿And preferred﴾, that is, he honored, put forward, and chose ﴿the worldly life﴾, by making the trace of the base, near-at-hand world greater in his estimation, because it was present before him, than the trace of the exalted Hereafter, because it was absent. So he was like the beasts, having no perception except of the present particulars, and he plunged into all of its affairs and turned away from preparing for the Hereafter through worship and the refinement of the soul, so he did not restrain his soul from desire.

Since man is held accountable for what he has earned, the verse traces his deeds to a consequence, stressing it to refute their denial: ﴿Indeed, the Blazing Fire [al-Jahim] is the abode﴾, that is, the fierce, intensely blazing Fire, its multitudes gathered against whoever enters it, ﴿it is the abode﴾, that is, none other than it is the dwelling-place for him. This is the view of the Basrans, that the pronoun is elided; according to the Kufans, the definite article "al" (alif-lam) takes the place of the pronoun. This is related by Abu Hayyan.

When he mentioned the transgressor, He followed him with the god-fearing one, saying: ﴿But as for he who feared the standing before his Lord﴾. Since that fear is directed at something that is connected to another thing, and for that reason is greater than fear of that thing itself, He said ﴿the standing before his Lord﴾, meaning his standing before the One who has done him good. When he remembers that goodness, he does not transgress, so how much less will he transgress when he remembers His majesty and His retribution? Or it may mean the place where he stands before Him, and the time. If he fears that standing, then what do you think of fear of the One before whom he stands? This is not done except by one who truly affirms the Return.

When He mentioned the fear, He mentioned what results from it and did not make it the cause of it, so that you understand that each of the two is a separate matter in its own right, even though it is distinct from the other. So He said: (p-244) ﴿and restrained the soul﴾, meaning the soul that is inclined to rivalry, ﴿from desire﴾, meaning everything it desires, for this does not lead to good, because the Fire is surrounded by desires, and the whole Sharia is built on what opposes natural inclination and what souls desire. These are the prohibitions with which the Fire is surrounded, for it is surrounded by desires. Al-Razi said: desire (hawa) is the blameworthy appetite that opposes the commands of the Sharia. Al-Junayd said: when the soul opposes its desire, its illness becomes its cure. This indicates that he did not prefer the worldly life. Thus the verse is of the type called ihtibak (a rhetorical device in which one of two opposites is mentioned and the other is implied): He mentioned "transgressed" as evidence of its opposite in the second place, and the prohibition of desire in the second place as evidence of preferring this world in the first place.

When the context is one of encouragement (targhib), he linked the recompense to the deed, as he had done in the context of warning (tarhib), so he said, and he emphasized it to refute the disbelievers: ﴿Indeed, Paradise﴾, i.e., the garden that gathers everything one desires, ﴿it is﴾, i.e., exclusively, ﴿the refuge﴾, i.e., for him; he does not take refuge in anything other than it. And this is the state of those who are mindful (al-muraqibin).

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 79, verse 42:

When He had divided them into this division, which conveys that this is something unavoidable, He resumed mentioning their mockery, expressing wonder at them, and said: ﴿They ask you﴾, i.e., the Quraysh, in a manner of renewal and continuity, asking in mockery, denial and disbelief: ﴿about the Hour﴾, i.e., the final resurrection, because of how often you threaten them with it, "concerning our command." Since the question about it was vague (p. 245), He clarified it by His saying: ﴿When is its appointed time?﴾, i.e., [at what] time its mooring [occurs], i.e., its occurrence, or its fixity and settling.

Since presenting this in such a way conveys disapproval of them in this question, and it is known that he would say: "They ask me, and perhaps his noble soul would be moved to answer them, out of his eagerness for their conversion and compassion for them," He restrained him from that and openly expressed disapproval with His saying: ﴿Why (fīma) are you (anta) in mention of it (min dhikrāhā)?﴾ That is, in what matter are you concerned with its great mention, so that you would know it and explain its time to them out of eagerness for their conversion? That would not benefit knowledge of it.

Then he defined it by what admits no addition, from what the preceding sentence indicated, namely that its knowledge is not possible for anyone other than Him, glory be to Him and exalted, so He said: ﴿To your Lord﴾, that is, the One who is good to you alone, ﴿is its finality﴾, that is, the end of its knowledge and of all its affair.

When their ultimate aim was to say, "He is only fabricating it from his own self," He turned the matter back upon them and said: ﴿You are only a warner﴾, that is, O most noble of the messengers, ﴿a warner﴾, meaning one who gives warning in the manner of certainty that cannot be avoided, with your knowledge of what you warn of, the knowledge in which there is no doubt. ﴿For whoever fears it﴾, that is, for whoever has the capacity to fear it greatly, so that he acts for it, given his knowledge that it will surely come and his knowledge that he will surely die, and his knowledge that everything whose occurrence is certain is near. This does not fit specifying its time, for whoever has the capacity for fear is only increased in fear by its being vague, while others are only increased by it in audacity and transgression. So We did not send you except to warn of it, not to inform of its time, for the first kind of warning benefits, not the second. You are in nothing of what they describe you with, as a lie from them, because We do not send messengers except as bearers of good tidings and warners, and you have not been sent to determine the time of the Hour or a knowledge that He has kept specific. He restricted it to whoever fears because others do not benefit from his warning, so it is as though the warning did not reach them at all. For this meaning He added an indication that he is deeply engaged in warning whoever fears; as for others, he is a warner to them in a general sense, meaning that the appearance of warning occurs for them, since he warns them in the sense that the essence of warning does not occur for them.

When He had established that he is a warner, and the most fearsome warning is haste, He said, beginning a new statement, belittling the worldly life for them and making them ignore it: ﴿As if they, on the day they see it,﴾ that is, these deniers of the truth of the warning about it, ﴿will not have remained﴾ that is, in the world or in the graves, ﴿except for an evening﴾ that is, from midday until sunset.

Since they were not certain of anything they said, He said: ﴿or its morning﴾ that is, the morning of one of the evenings [p. 247], which is from dawn until midday, while the evening is what follows that. The morning is attributed to the evening because it is part of the day, and attribution (idafah) takes place with the slightest connection, which here is that both belong to one day. So what is meant is an hour of a day, its beginning or its end. They did not complete a full day, nor did they join its two ends. This is like what the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "The likeness of this world compared to the Hereafter is only like one of you dipping his finger in the sea; let him see what it returns with." This is an expression for us in terms of what we perceive, to bring it closer to our minds, although the principle is that there is no ratio between what is finite and what is infinite. Moreover, the disbelievers also consider the duration of their stay to be short. So they are of various kinds: some say, "You did not remain except ten," some say, "You did not remain except a day," and some are bewildered and say, "Ask those who count." Or these were their statements. The truth in this matter is what God has informed of, not attributed to their statements: that what passed for them, compared with what is to come, is as if it were an hour of a day in relation to a full day, as He said in Surah Yunus, upon whom be peace, ﴿And on the day He gathers them, as if they had not remained except an hour of the day, recognizing one another among themselves﴾ [Yunus: 45]. Also, some of them say this as well, as He said in Surah al-Mu'minun when He said, ﴿How many years did you remain on the earth?﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 112] ﴿They said: We remained a day or part of a day; so ask those who count﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 113]. This is in relation to what was revealed to them about what they would face, which has no end; or because, when the blast of Isrāfīl, upon whom be peace, pulled them by the power of might from their graves in a violent pull, they stood up and saw those terrors and knew what they would face of dread, they regarded the duration of their stay before that as short, because whoever has enjoyed something finds its duration short. And they had enjoyed that, even if it was among the bitterest of bitter things, in comparison with what they encountered. Thus its last part returned upon its first by the Resurrection, and its joints were wrapped, with the souls that blame joined to what connects them, and it was linked to the first of what follows it from the side of fear and remembrance. How good is its connection! Glory be to Him who made it a mutual embrace of its pauses and its readings, and sent it down as gardens whose paths and returns are firmly arranged. And God, glory be to Him and exalted, is the One who grants success to what is right, and to Him is the return and the final place.
